40.0.0.en: 1- “In waiting I waited for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.”

40.0.1.en: 1- It is clear that David was subjected to many wrongs from those who wronged him, but he bore them and waited a long time. He confirms this by his saying “In waiting I waited”... and this confirms David's faith, his hope in God and his reliance on Him. For he kept silent and did not murmur, and surrendered his life to God and awaited His intervention, because of his confidence that He would surely deliver him.

40.0.2.en: 2- God's tenderness and humility appear in His inclining toward David and His care to hear his prayers and his cry; He did not neglect him because He loves him. And David here is a type of Christ, who bore the sufferings for our sake and awaited the revealing of His glory after the torments and the Cross, and appeared in His Resurrection.

40.1.0.en: 2- “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings.”

40.1.1.en: 1- David likens his suffering and afflictions to being in a pit, that is, a deep hole from which he cannot get out. He also says that this pit is full of mire, from which he cannot get out, but if he tried to get out he would sink deeper in it; so he surely needs the intervention of God, who stretched out His hand and brought him up.

40.1.2.en: 2- Falling into the pit and the mire expresses David's falling into sin, and his inability to get out of it by his own strength although he had repented of it; so God stretched out His hand, brought him up from it and forgave his sins.

40.1.3.en: 3- God was not content to bring David up out of the pit, but lifted him onto a rock, that is, solid ground and not like mire. So David was able to triumph with confidence and strength, and even to walk with strong steps, advancing and succeeding; because God, when He saw his striving, established his steps so that they became stronger. And the rock is a type of Christ, on whom His children lean throughout their lives (1 Cor 10:4).

40.2.0.en: 3- “And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.”

40.2.1.en: 1- In addition to God's delivering David from the pit, He pushed him onto the path of positivity, by teaching him a new song that expresses new feelings, and a great joy that David felt, so he praised God, who cares for His children, rescues them from all problems and dangers, and forgives them all their sins.

40.2.2.en: 2- When the people saw God's wonderful work with David they feared God, since they felt that He is stronger than all the gods, that He is able to do all things, and that He alone can be relied upon in all situations; so David's faith and reliance became an example to all around him.

40.2.3.en: Wait for the Lord when a problem befalls you, and persevere in your prayers, confident that He is near you and will surely intervene and rescue you, whatever the threats of the wicked.

40.3.0.en: 4- “Blessed is that man that maketh the LORD his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies.”

40.3.1.en: The proud (ghataris): the singular is ghatris, meaning the arrogant and conceited.

40.3.2.en: 1- David glorifies the man who relies on God, in order to call all people to rely on God, and by this man he means himself, so as to strengthen all the righteous in the face of the wrongs of the wicked.

40.3.3.en: 2- David supports and blesses the man who relies on God, so that he may not look to the proud and lying wicked, nor to the great ones of the world who have authority, but may trust in God, in whose hand are all things.

40.3.4.en: 3- Whoever does not rely on God meets misery instead of blessedness; for when the people of God did not rely on Him, and feared the inhabitants of the land of Canaan, God deprived them of entering it and they died in the wilderness of Sinai (Num 14:22, 23).

40.4.0.en: 5- “Many, O LORD my God, are thy wonderful works which thou hast done, and thy thoughts which are to us-ward: they cannot be reckoned up in order unto thee: if I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be numbered.”

40.4.1.en: They cannot be reckoned up: they cannot be counted.

40.4.2.en: 1- David meditated on God's care for him and for His people throughout history, and found that God's works are wonderful, surpassing the mind, and so many that he cannot count them. And His thoughts and arrangements toward His children are very great.

40.4.3.en: 2- David's purpose in meditating on God's works is to tell of them to others in order to glorify God. But he found it impossible to count them, and therefore was content to speak of some of them, which is what he was able to enumerate and speak about.

40.5.0.en: 6- “Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required. 7- Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me.”

40.5.1.en: Volume (scroll): a piece of skin or papyrus on which writings were written in ancient times.

40.5.2.en: 1- David made clear that God asks for obedience to His commandments before the offering of sacrifices. And God opens David's ears to hear and obey, because obedience is better than the offering of sacrifice. And offering sacrifices without obeying God's commandments profits nothing. The meaning is not the rejection of offering sacrifices, because God commanded them, but He wants to declare that obedience to God's commandments surpasses every sacrifice, whether a burnt offering or a sin offering. For by obedience man sacrifices his own will and prefers the will of God to what he himself wants.

40.5.3.en: 2- David spoke in the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who says to the Father that He took no pleasure in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, because they were merely a type, but His pleasure was in the coming of Christ and His Incarnation, for He is the sacrifice that was prefigured, who would be offered on the Cross, as mentioned in the volume of the book, that is, the prophecies of the Old Testament. And the Incarnation of Christ is the obedience of the Son to the Father, so Christ's obedience is better than the burnt offerings and sin offerings, and Christ's coming by His Incarnation is the fulfilment of the Father's will; therefore He said, “Lo, I come.”

40.6.0.en: 8- “I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is in the midst of my bowels.”

40.6.1.en: 1- David loved God, and God's law became his delight; so he held fast to it and applied it in his life, and he took pleasure in carrying it out, because it had become in his heart and bowels, that is, he felt it, and afterward it appeared in his conduct. So the believers feel in every generation, and the word of God becomes lived in their hearts and conduct, and their life becomes a lived Gospel.

40.6.2.en: 2- This verse is a clear prophecy about Christ, who became incarnate to fulfil the pleasure and satisfaction of the Father and to do His will, which is the redemption of mankind. And God's law was in His bowels, that is, His depths; for He is the Word of God, the Second Hypostasis, who became incarnate that we might see in Him how the law is applied in practical life.

40.7.0.en: 9- “I have preached the Lord in the great congregation: lo, I have not refrained my lips, O LORD, thou knowest. 10- I have not hid thy righteousness within my heart; I have declared thy faithfulness and thy salvation: I have not concealed thy lovingkindness and thy truth from the great congregation.”

40.7.1.en: 1- David declares that he has preached God in the midst of his people, who are the great congregation, whether by killing Goliath, or by his service with King Saul, or by his bearing Saul's pursuit, or when he reigned over the people of God and continued to hold fast to God's righteousness, so he spoke with his lips and taught love to all around him. And God knows David's heart, that it is with God, and not merely words he utters with his lips (Acts 13:22).

40.7.2.en: 2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who preached not only among the Jewish people but among the Gentiles also, for He offered righteousness and love on the Cross in His death, being the Righteous One without sin, for the redemption of all mankind. And He preached in His life on earth with His lips, which signify justice and mercy, which are perfected in His Incarnation and redemption and all His words. And the Father knows how the Son is the Righteous, the Holy One.

40.7.3.en: 3- Christ still speaks of His faithfulness and salvation through the Apostles, the priests and the servants to this day by the work of the Holy Spirit, not only in the words of the Evangelist, but also in the lived life of His children. And He also does not conceal His mercy and His truth, that is, God's forgiveness and support of His children, in addition to His warnings so that His children may repent. This is in the great congregation, that is, in the whole world for Christians, that they may live in purity, and for the whole world, that it may believe and repent.

40.7.4.en: Proclaim the voice of God to all around you by holding fast to God's commandments, keeping away from all evil, and offering your love to every person, so that you become light to the world and salt to the earth.

40.8.s.en: (3) A request for deliverance from evils

40.8.0.en: 11- “But thou, O Lord, withhold not thy compassion from me; let thy mercy and thy truth always help me.”

40.8.1.en: 1- David's humility appears in his asking God to have compassion on him; he is like the tax collector who humbly asked for God's mercy and obtained His forgiveness, and this confirms the importance of humility in the spiritual life.

40.8.2.en: 2- David relies on God's mercy in forgiving his sins and supporting him, in addition to God's truth, that is, His justice, which is firm in the way of righteousness and judges evil to be void; so by mercy and truth David triumphs over Satan and lives with God unshaken by the success of the wicked, and even arrives at complete victory in eternal life.

40.9.0.en: 12- “For innumerable evils have compassed me about: mine iniquities have taken hold upon me, so that I am not able to look up; they are more than the hairs of mine head: therefore my heart faileth me.”

40.9.2.en: 1- David remembers the wrongs of his enemies toward him, and declares that evils have compassed him on every side, and that the cause of this is his sins which have compassed him. This shows that David is a repentant man, who attributes the afflictions to the multitude of his sins, and by these feelings of remorse he obtains God's mercies and forgiveness.

40.9.3.en: 2- When David's sins multiplied they took away his ability to discern, so that he no longer saw God, and also his feelings, that is, his heart, left him, that is, he no longer felt God as he used to in the past; so he is in severe suffering because of the multitude of his sins, but when he repented he regained his spiritual enlightenment.

40.10.0.en: 13- “Be pleased, O LORD, to deliver me: O LORD, make haste to help me.”

40.10.1.en: 1- The verses from this verse to the end of the psalm are repeated in Psalm 70. We find in them a supplication from David to the holy God to condescend and be pleased to deliver him from his many sins to which he referred in the previous verse. So David continues in his humility and self-abasement before God, but in a firm hope that He will lift from him the continual afflictions that surround him.

40.10.2.en: 2- Because of Job's great distress over his sins, he declares his swift need for God's intervention, that He may lift them from him and restore to him his sonship and his relationship with God; so He supports him lest he fall a second time.

40.11.0.en: 14- “Let them be ashamed and confounded together that seek after my soul to destroy it; let them be driven backward and put to shame that delight in my hurt. 15- Let them be desolate for a reward of their shame that say unto me, Aha, aha.”

40.11.1.en: Let them be desolate: let them fear and tremble.

40.11.2.en: Aha, aha: an expression of gloating.

40.11.3.en: 1- David prays for the wicked who want to destroy him, not asking for vengeance on them, but that shame and disgrace may overtake them, so that they may know the result of their evils, and turn away from evil and repent, and thus return to God; he prays for them and does not gloat over them. Rather, he asks that they be driven backward from their sins, that is, that they repent of them.

40.11.4.en: 2- When the demons see the shame of the wicked, who tried to harm and destroy David, they fear and tremble, for they see that their earlier gloating over David, by their saying “Aha, aha,” profited nothing. So they gloated of old over Adam at his fall, but Christ became incarnate and redeemed mankind.

40.12.0.en: 16- “Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: let such as love thy salvation say, ‘The LORD be magnified.’”

40.12.1.en: 1- David believed that God is his Savior, so he desired that all the children of God who seek Him share his joy. David feels his membership in the congregation of the people of God, and wants them to share together in joys and sorrows. And in the midst of these joys and their enjoyment of salvation they magnify the Lord, the giver of this salvation.

40.12.2.en: 2- David's love for those who seek the Lord appears in his calling them to joy, “rejoice and be glad,” in God, and to take refuge in Him in all their needs, “all those that seek thee,” then they praise God and magnify Him, “The LORD be magnified,” and finally they long for His eternal salvation, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven, “such as love thy salvation.”

40.13.0.en: 17- “But I am poor and needy; yet the Lord thinketh upon me: thou art my help and my deliverer; make no tarrying, O my God.”

40.13.1.en: 1- David concludes his psalm with humility, declaring that he is poor and needy, that is, he has no hope or strength except in God his helper. And because of his humility he obtains God's great mercies, unlike the demons and their followers, the proud and gloating wicked, who are put to shame and disgrace.

40.13.2.en: 2- David also concludes his psalm with prayer, asking God's help quickly, because the affliction still surrounds him, and he trusts that God will intervene, because David has a personal relationship and boldness with God, so he says to Him “my help and my deliverer .. my God.” So also Moses concluded his song after crossing the Red Sea with prayer and the glorifying of God (Ex 15).

40.13.3.en: To the extent that you humble yourself, your prayers reach God and you obtain all help, and He even hastens to you more than you imagine.

40.13.4.en: The blessed and the traitors, to the choirmaster. A psalm of David “Blessed is he that considereth the poor” (v. 1) Introduction:

40.13.5.en: 1- Its writer is the prophet David.

40.13.6.en: 2- When was it written? During the rebellion of Absalom against his father David. It appears that David was ill, and his illness helped Absalom's betrayal of him, since the management of affairs in the country was shaken, and Absalom exploited it to win people to himself and carry out a revolt against his father. And the psalm speaks about Ahithophel, the betrayer of David.

40.13.7.en: 3- This psalm calls for care for the poor.

40.13.8.en: 4- This psalm is one of the Messianic psalms, because it speaks of the wicked's opposition to Christ, the sufferings of Christ, the betrayal of Judas, and the Resurrection of Christ. Christ cited this psalm when speaking about the betrayal of Judas (Jn 13:18), and the Apostle Peter also cited it (Acts 1:16).

40.13.9.en: 5- There is a similarity between this psalm and the first psalm, since both speak of the wicked's opposition to Christ, or their opposition to the righteous, and the victory of the righteous in the end.

40.13.10.en: 6- The psalm is considered a personal lament of David.

40.13.11.en: 7- This psalm was chanted in the temple, so it is one of the liturgical psalms.

40.13.12.en: 8- This psalm is the last psalm in the first section of the Psalms (Ps 1-41), according to the division of the Jews, who divided the Psalms into five sections. And this psalm ends, like the end of the four sections, with the word Amen in its last verse.

40.13.13.en: 9- This psalm is found in the Agpeya in the prayer of the Third Hour.
